But I am not blind, I know for a fact the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. They are even keeping tabs on my cleaning routes to see if I am taking proper care of my husband. \n\nWhich is just ridiculous because I take care of everything. I clean houses for a living, you know, I am a housekeeper. Just on Tuesday I was doing a deep clean over on Elm Street, and the lady there has these huge, heavy velvet curtains. You wouldn't believe how much dust they hold. I had to take them down and haul them outside to beat them, and my shoulder has been aching ever since. My husband used to help me with the heavy lifting before he got bad, but now it is just me doing it all. We used to have a beautiful garden, too, lots of tomatoes and squash. The bugs got to the squash this year though... wait, what was I saying? \n\nOh, right, why I came in. But yes, they think I am making up the agency people watching my routes, but I know what I see.\n\nDoctor: When you say the hospital people and agency are watching your house and monitoring your cleaning routes, do you think there might be any other explanation for what you're experiencing, or are you completely certain this is actually happening?\n\nPatient: No, no, there is no other explanation. I am completely certain. Like I said, people keep acting like I am just imagining it all, but I know for a fact the hospital people and the agency folks are watching the house. They are monitoring my cleaning routes to see if I am taking proper care of my husband, and I am not blind. \n\nI mean, I see their cars. Just yesterday, there was a dark blue sedan parked right across from the Miller place—that is my Thursday morning job. Mrs. Miller has this beautiful antique grandfather clock in her front hallway. It chimes every quarter hour, which honestly drives me a little crazy when I am trying to mop the hardwood floors. I use a special oil soap there, and it takes a lot of focus so it doesn't streak. You have to go exactly with the grain of the wood, you know? My mother taught me that. She was an absolute stickler for clean floors. We used to scrub them on our hands and knees every Saturday morning before we were allowed to watch cartoons... \n\nWait, what did you ask me? Oh, about being sure. Yes, I am absolutely sure they are watching me. I know what I see, doctor.\n\nDoctor: Besides seeing those cars watching you, have you ever heard voices speaking to you when no one else was around, or seen things that others couldn't explain?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. I don't usually tell people this because they look at me funny, but even when the house is completely quiet, I hear a woman's voice. She's usually right near the kitchen window, clear as day, like she's standing right next to me. She tells me to check the locks or move my husband's pills. \n\nSpeaking of the kitchen window, I really need to wash those curtains. They're a yellow gingham, very cheerful, but they catch all the grease from the stove. I usually take them down and soak them in the bathtub with a little bleach and detergent. I had to keep shooing him away... \n\nWhat was I saying? Oh, the voice. Yes, the woman by the window. I definitely hear her, clear as if she's right there.\n\nDoctor: When did you first start hearing that woman's voice and noticing people watching your house? The voices and the feeling that people are watching us, I'd say it's been happening for about 11 months now. \n\nIt started around the same time I was doing that big spring cleaning job for the Petersons. Oh, they have this lovely house, but the dust! You wouldn't believe it. They have these intricate baseboards, you know, the kind with all the little grooves? And their cat, Mr. Whiskers, he just sat there watching me the whole time, judging me, I swear. Cats are like that, aren't they? They just stare at you. Reminds me of my aunt's cat, Barnaby. He used to hide under the sofa and swipe at your ankles when you walked by. We had to start wearing thick socks just to go into the living room...\n\nOh, dear, I lost my train of thought again. But yes, about 11 months, that's how long it's been since the voice and the watching started.\n\nDoctor: Besides the stress from worrying about being watched and hearing the voice, have you been able to keep up with your housekeeping jobs and take care of your husband and home the way you normally would, or has this all made it harder for you to do those things?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's definitely made things harder, yes. My cleaning agency actually took away my supervisory routes. They said the clients and my coworkers felt they couldn't rely on my work the way they used to, which is just ridiculous because I am very thorough. I mean, I always make sure to use the right polish on the brass fixtures. You can't just use any all-purpose cleaner on real brass, it tarnishes it terribly. I learned that the hard way when I first started out, working at this old Victorian bed and breakfast. The owner, Mrs. Higgins, she had these gorgeous brass doorknobs on every single door. There must have been thirty doors in that house. I spent a whole afternoon polishing them once, and my hands smelled like metal for two days straight. No matter how much lemon juice and salt I scrubbed them with, the smell just lingered... \n\nOh, but you were asking about my husband, weren't you? Yes, well, at home, my husband and our pastor have had to step in a lot more lately. They say I'm not keeping up with the caregiving and the household stuff safely. Pastor Thomas even started bringing over casseroles on Tuesdays. He makes a lovely tuna noodle casserole, though he puts peas in it, and I always pick the peas out. I just can't stand the texture of cooked peas, they get so mushy. But yes, they've been having to help out because things have just been... slipping, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: When you're talking with someone, do they ever tell you that it's hard to follow what you're saying, or that you jump around between different topics? Does that happen to you often?\n\nPatient: Well... yes, I suppose they do. It's very frustrating because it all connects perfectly fine in my head. But when I try to explain what is happening, the words just sort of run away from me. I'll start out talking about my husband's heart pills, and then somehow I'm on about the church schedule, or the numbers on my client list, and people tell me they just can't follow me at all. \n\nSpeaking of the church schedule, they just changed the time for the Sunday evening service, and Pastor Thomas's wife, Brenda, she handles all the printed bulletins. She started printing them on this pale blue paper. It's a nice color, robin's egg blue, but she uses this font that's terribly hard to read. It's all curly and squiggly. I told her, Brenda, the older folks in the congregation can't read this, but she just smiled and said it looked elegant. Elegant! What good is elegant if Mrs. Gable misses choir practice because she thought a three was an eight? Mrs. Gable is a sweet lady, though. She makes the absolute best rhubarb pie for the summer potlucks. I always try to get a slice before it's gone, but her grandson usually eats half the tin himself. He's a big boy, plays football for the high school, so I suppose he needs the calories, but still... \n\nOh, dear. I'm doing it right now, aren't I? Jumping around. But yes, people do tell me it's hard to follow what I'm saying.\n\nDoctor: When you first started noticing the voices and the people watching you about 11 months ago, were you already having trouble organizing your thoughts and jumping between topics the way you do now, or did that confusion with your speech come later?\n\nPatient: Well, I... I'm not entirely sure, to be honest. It's hard to pin down exactly when the talking got so muddled. I mean, 11 months ago, that was right around the time I was doing the Petersons' spring cleaning, like I said. And the voices were definitely there then. But the speech thing... I don't know if it started exactly then or a bit later. \n\nTime just gets away from you, doesn't it? Like how it's already November, and I haven't even thought about getting the winter coats out of the cedar chest. I always keep them in the cedar chest to keep the moths away. Moths are just terrible around here. Last year, they got into my husband's favorite wool sweater, the green one he wears when he goes ice fishing. He was so upset. He loves ice fishing, though I can't understand why anyone would want to sit on a frozen lake for hours. He takes this little thermos of coffee, but it always goes cold by noon. I bought him a new thermos for Christmas, one of those expensive vacuum-sealed ones, but he said it was too heavy to carry out on the ice... \n\nI'm sorry, what were we talking about? The confusion with my speech... I just really can't say for sure if it started right at the same time as the voices or if it came on later. It's all just a bit of a blur.\n\nDoctor: When you think back to about 11 months ago when this all started, did the voices and the feeling of being watched come on suddenly—like one day you noticed them and they were just there—or did they start very gradually, getting a little bit stronger or more noticeable day by day?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's hard to remember exactly how it started. You really need a good, sturdy shoe when you're on your feet all day, especially on hard floors. Tile is the worst for your back. The Petersons have this beautiful Spanish tile in their kitchen, but sweeping it is a nightmare because the dirt gets caught in the grout lines... \n\nBut anyway, about the voices and the watching... I really couldn't tell you if it was sudden or gradual. It's just too hard to remember how it all began.\n\nDoctor: When you're having a conversation with someone, do they seem frustrated or confused because your thoughts jump around so much, or do they mostly understand what you're saying even though it might take you a while to get to the point?\n\nPatient: Well, I think... yes, people definitely get confused.
